intended_object: Take a Dynkin system d on α and a set s ∈ d. The intended object is the Dynkin system D_s = {t ⊆ α | t ∩ s ∈ d}. This is the standard auxiliary system in the proof of Dynkin's π-λ theorem. I inferred this from the docstring, the name and its use in `generate_inter` in the same file.
explanation:
The body defines the predicate `Has t := d.Has (t ∩ s)`, so it is exactly the set {t | t ∩ s ∈ d}. This is the textbook construction (for example Kallenberg's or Billingsley's proof of the π-λ theorem). Its closure properties are proved correctly:
- **Empty set:** ∅ ∩ s = ∅ is in d.
- **Complements:** tᶜ ∩ s = (t ∩ s)ᶜ \ sᶜ. Since sᶜ ⊆ (t ∩ s)ᶜ, this set is in d by closure under proper differences.
- **Countable disjoint unions:** (⋃ fᵢ) ∩ s = ⋃ (fᵢ ∩ s), and the sets fᵢ ∩ s are pairwise disjoint.

The only use of the definition is in `generate_inter`, the core of the π-λ theorem, which is exactly the textbook role of this system.

The docstring's phrase "{s ∩ t | t ∈ d}" is imprecise. Read literally as a family of subsets of α, it is not a Dynkin system unless s = univ, because it would have to contain univ = ∅ᶜ. So the phrase loosely describes the standard construction rather than a different object the definition fails to match. Since s ∈ d is required, the construction lives at its natural generality: any Dynkin system on any type. Mathlib has no more general counterpart.
